position.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes status-driven visibility, positioning the machine as a premium, visible purchase tied to income. Use the proposed purchase-test to validate demand before full investment.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

T1.claim: Home barista consumers will adopt premium espresso machines if they perceive them as a status symbol, because visible consumption of high-quality coffee increases purchase intent when income is tied to social status.
T1.who_benefits: Simonelli Group would capture value through premium pricing and brand positioning as a status product.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers link purchasing visible, status-driven products to personal prestige, leading them to choose machines that signal affluence.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can command higher prices and build brand loyalty by marketing machines as exclusive, status-driven items.
assumptions: Consumers associate visible coffee purchases with social status.
Income is a primary driver of purchase decisions for high-end coffee equipment.
Simonelli can effectively communicate status positioning to consumers.
predictions: In a test offering a premium machine at a higher price when income is linked to status, purchase intent will be significantly higher than when income is randomly assigned.
Consumers who view the machine as a visible purchase will show higher purchase intent than those who keep it private.
T1.first_claim: Home barista consumers will adopt premium espresso machines if they perceive them as a status symbol, because visible consumption of high-quality coffee increases purchase intent when income is tied to social status.

T2.claim: Home barista consumers will adopt premium espresso machines because they value convenience and ease of use, not because they view it as a status symbol.
T2.who_benefits: Simonelli Group would capture value through higher margins on simplified, user-friendly machines that reduce purchase friction.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers prioritize quick, hassle-free preparation over signaling prestige, especially when the machine is marketed as easy to operate.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Simonelli can price machines at premium levels while emphasizing convenience, leveraging its existing professional reputation for reliability.
assumptions: Convenience is a primary purchase driver for home barista equipment.
Status is a secondary, less influential factor in purchase decisions.
Simonelli can effectively communicate convenience through marketing.
predictions: In a test offering a premium machine with simplified controls, purchase intent will be higher than when controls are complex.
Consumers who emphasize convenience will show higher purchase intent than those who focus on status.
T2.first_claim: Home barista consumers will adopt premium espresso machines because they value convenience and ease of use, not because they view it as a status symbol.

assessments.quote: Making consumption choices visible leads to a large increase in demand when income is linked to status, but not otherwise.
assessments.does_not_show: It does not show that Simonelli's machines are the specific product that drives this effect, nor that consumers would purchase them at a premium price.

assessments.quote: The approximately $3,900 machine (United States market) represents the smallest and least expensive machine in the growing La Marzocco Home espresso machine line.
assessments.does_not_show: It does not show that convenience is the primary purchase driver, nor that Simonelli's machines meet that criterion.

X1.name: Status vs Convenience Purchase Test
X1.method: Online choice experiment with simulated purchase of a premium home espresso machine.
X1.sample: 300 adult participants recruited via an online panel, balanced for age, gender, and income levels.
X1.measure: Purchase intent measured on a 7-point scale (1 = very unlikely, 7 = very likely) and actual willingness to pay (WTP) in euros.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants who view the machine as a visible, status-driven purchase (linked to income) will report higher purchase intent and WTP than those who keep it private.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants who emphasize convenience (simplified controls, quick prep) will report higher purchase intent and WTP than those who focus on status.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent for the status condition exceeds the average for the convenience condition by at least 1.5 points on the 7-point scale, proceed to develop a status-driven consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 1.5 points, proceed to develop a convenience-driven proposition. If both conditions are equal, do not invest in either proposition and conduct further market research.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-SIMO-UPDATE) does not address purchase drivers (status vs convenience) but tests a learning offer among enthusiasts. It does not provide evidence for or against T1, so the theory remains unchanged.

final.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes status-driven visibility, positioning the machine as a premium, visible purchase tied to income. Use the proposed purchase-test to validate demand before full investment.
final.target_customer: Affluent home barista enthusiasts who value visible, status-driven consumption of high-quality coffee.
final.value_proposition: A premium home espresso machine marketed as an exclusive, visible status item that signals affluence and aligns with the growing prosumer market.
final.next_action: Run the 12‑week, €20,000 online choice experiment with 300 participants to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay under status and convenience conditions.
final.uncertainty: The actual size of the home barista market and Simonelli’s ability to capture value at premium prices remain uncertain. The test will clarify whether status or convenience drives purchase decisions.
would_change_if: If the test shows the convenience condition outperforming the status condition by at least 1.5 points, the recommendation would shift to a convenience‑driven proposition.
If the test yields no significant difference between status and convenience conditions, further market research would be needed before committing to either proposition.

The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

position.recommendation: Simonelli Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes lifestyle and social sharing, leveraging its premium design and connectivity to capture the growing home barista market. This aligns with the observed demand for premium, Instagram-friendly machines and the company’s existing focus on design-forward products.

frame.objective: Determine whether Simonelli Group should invest in creating a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case beyond its current professional espresso-equipment offering, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Current reach to individual buyers is unknown and must be discovered.
Any recommendation must be justified by evidence of consumer demand, willingness to pay, and Simonelli’s ability to capture value.
Alternatives include expanding the existing professional line, creating a new consumer product, targeting a different customer segment, or maintaining the current portfolio.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case (e.g., home barista, travel, or small office) with a new product or marketing approach.
2) Expand the existing professional line with consumer‑focused features (e.g., simplified controls, compact design) without creating a new product.
3) Target a different customer segment (e.g., coffee shops, hotels, or retail consumers) with a differentiated offering, leveraging existing or new distribution channels.
4) Maintain the current portfolio and not pursue expansion, focusing resources on existing professional and commercial segments.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Test: Lifestyle vs. Convenience
X1.method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a design-forward, premium-priced home barista machine with social-sharing features (e.g., Instagram-friendly design, connectivity). Group B sees a compact, easy-to-use machine with time-saving features (e.g., quick brewing, compact size). Both groups are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the top reason for choosing the product.
X1.sample: 300 adult consumers interested in coffee, recruited via an online panel. 150 per group to ensure statistical power.
X1.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary reason for choosing the product (open-ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and will cite social sharing as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and will cite convenience as the primary reason.

X1.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 5.5), conclude that lifestyle/social-sharing motivation drives demand and T1 is more likely. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, conclude convenience drives demand and T2 is more likely. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-SIMO-UPDATE) does not address lifestyle/social-sharing motivation; it tests a learning proposition among home barista enthusiasts, not the broader home barista market. Therefore it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Simonelli Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes lifestyle and social sharing, leveraging its premium design and connectivity to capture the growing home barista market.

final.value_proposition: A premium, design-forward home espresso machine that combines functionality with Instagram-friendly aesthetics and connectivity, allowing consumers to showcase their coffee experience and connect with a community.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Consumer Preference Test (X1) to validate purchase intent and primary motivation (lifestyle vs. convenience). If the test confirms a significant lifestyle advantage, proceed to develop the differentiated product; otherwise,

would_change_if: If the test shows a convenience advantage (Group B's purchase intent exceeds Group A by at least 5 points), the recommendation would shift to a convenience-focused proposition.

arguments.name: Consumer Preference Test: Lifestyle vs. Convenience
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated product offers. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups. Group A sees a design-forward, premium-priced home barista machine with social-sharing features (e.g., Instagram-friendly design, connectivity). Group B sees a compact, easy-to-use machine with time-saving features (e.g., quick brewing, compact size). Both groups are asked to indicate purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑10) and to state the top reason for choosing the product.
arguments.sample: 300 adult consumers interested in coffee, recruited via an online panel. 150 per group to ensure statistical power.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent score (1‑10) and primary reason for choosing the product (open-ended).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will have higher purchase intent and will cite social sharing as the primary reason.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will have higher purchase intent and will cite convenience as the primary reason.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average purchase intent score for Group A is at least 5 points higher than Group B (i.e., Group A’s average ≥ 5.5), conclude that lifestyle/social-sharing motivation drives demand and T1 is more likely. If Group B’s average is at least 5 points higher, conclude convenience drives demand and T2 is more likely. If the difference is ≤ 1.5 points, both theories remain plausible and further testing is needed.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Simonelli Group should invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes lifestyle and social sharing, leveraging its premium design and connectivity to capture the growing home barista market. This aligns with the observed demand for premium, Instagram-friendly machines and the company’s existing focus on design-forward products.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 32 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 72 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

X1.name: Willingness-to-Pay Survey for Home Barista Segment
X1.method: Online survey with a controlled experiment. Recruit 300 home barista consumers (self-identified) from Europe. Randomly assign participants to one of two conditions: Condition A (lifestyle positioning) or Condition B (functional positioning). In Condition A, participants view a product description emphasizing lifestyle, quality, and convenience. In Condition B, they view the same description emphasizing functionality, performance, and price. Both conditions present the same product (e.g., a compact espresso machine). Participants indicate their maximum price they would pay and likelihood to purchase. Secondary measure: self-reported coffee consumption frequency.
X1.sample: 300 home barista consumers (self-identified) from Europe, recruited via online panels.
X1.measure: Maximum price willingness to pay (EUR) and purchase intent (1‑10 scale).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Condition A will show higher maximum price willingness to pay and higher purchase intent than Condition B.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Condition B will show higher maximum price willingness to pay and higher purchase intent than Condition A.

X1.decision_rule: If the average maximum price willingness to pay in Condition A exceeds Condition B by at least 15% (e.g., Condition A: €120 vs Condition B: €105), proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition. If the difference is less than 15%, do not invest in a new consumer proposition and focus on existing professional segments.

revisions.reason: The simulated result (SYN-SIMO-UPDATE) tests the incremental effect of a learning offer among home espresso enthusiasts, not the demand for a differentiated consumer proposition. It does not address whether home barista consumers are willing to pay a premium for a lifestyle proposition, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. The evidence shows Simonelli already sells a domestic flagship machine and plans a compact coffee grinder, but it does not demonstrate that home barista consumers are willing to pay a premium for a lifestyle proposition. The market is small and unprofitable, and the company is focused on professional and commercial segments.
final.target_customer: Home barista consumers in Europe who self-identify as enthusiasts and are willing to invest in premium coffee equipment.
final.value_proposition: A differentiated consumer proposition that positions Simonelli's products as lifestyle essentials, offering quality, convenience, and a community experience, with premium pricing and brand storytelling.
final.next_action: Conduct the proposed willingness-to-pay survey (or a smaller pilot) to test the incremental effect of lifestyle positioning versus functional positioning among home barista consumers.
final.uncertainty: The size and profitability of the home barista market remain uncertain. The survey results will determine whether there is sufficient demand to justify investment.
would_change_if: If the survey shows a willingness-to-pay premium of at least 15% for a lifestyle-focused product, or if market research reveals a growing home barista segment with disposable income.
If new evidence shows a significant decline in consumer product performance or a shift in consumer preferences away from premium coffee equipment.

X1.name: Home Barista Preference Survey
X1.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home barista communities and asked to rank importance of professional taste, control, convenience, and price when choosing espresso equipment. They then select a preferred machine from a predefined set.
X1.sample: 300 home barista respondents (150 per arm) recruited via social media and coffee forums.
X1.measure: Percentage of respondents ranking professional taste and control highest, and percentage ranking convenience highest. Also, average willingness to pay (WTP) for each machine.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of respondents will rank professional taste and control highest, and the WTP for professional machines will be significantly higher than for convenience-focused machines.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of respondents will rank convenience highest, and the WTP for convenience-focused machines will be significantly higher than for professional machines.

X1.decision_rule: If the proportion of respondents ranking professional taste and control highest is at least 60% and the WTP for professional machines is at least 20% higher than for convenience-focused machines, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing professional taste and control. If convenience ranks highest and the WTP for convenience machines is at least 20% higher, develop a convenience-focused proposition. If neither condition is met, maintain the current portfolio.

arguments.name: Home Barista Preference Survey
arguments.method: Online survey with a choice-based conjoint design. Participants are recruited from home barista communities and asked to rank importance of professional taste, control, convenience, and price when choosing espresso equipment. They then select a preferred machine from a predefined set.
arguments.sample: 300 home barista respondents (150 per arm) recruited via social media and coffee forums.
arguments.measure: Percentage of respondents ranking professional taste and control highest, and percentage ranking convenience highest. Also, average willingness to pay (WTP) for each machine.

prediction_by_theory.T1: At least 60% of respondents will rank professional taste and control highest, and the WTP for professional machines will be significantly higher than for convenience-focused machines.
prediction_by_theory.T2: At least 60% of respondents will rank convenience highest, and the WTP for convenience-focused machines will be significantly higher than for professional machines.

arguments.decision_rule: If the proportion of respondents ranking professional taste and control highest is at least 60% and the WTP for professional machines is at least 20% higher than for convenience-focused machines, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer proposition emphasizing professional taste and control. If convenience ranks highest and the WTP for convenience machines is at least 20% higher, develop a convenience-focused proposition. If neither condition is met, maintain the current portfolio.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Invest in a differentiated consumer proposition that emphasizes professional taste, control, and ritual, targeting home baristas who value the authentic espresso experience. Use the proposed Home Barista Preference Survey to validate demand before committing resources.

result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

tool_result.title: Simulated home-barista learning proposition test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. Treat the following only as a what-if. In this hypothetical randomized study, 800 home espresso enthusiasts considering the same Simonelli single-group machine were assigned equally to two offers. Machine, brand, price, warranty, availability and total contact time were identical. One offer included a structured hands-on home-barista setup lesson; the other included an equal-length product-specification orientation without a skill lesson. There were no discounts. The outcome was a paid, refundable machine reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days, counted among all 400 assigned enthusiasts per arm. There were 72 reservations in the home-barista-lesson offer arm and 32 in the product-specification-orientation offer arm. This tests the incremental effect of this learning offer among recruited enthusiasts, not a need for a new machine, demand among ordinary coffee drinkers, commercial margins or lasting skill retention. It does not show that every hobby or status mechanism is true or false.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing B2B reputation and smart home integration capabilities. The test should validate willingness to pay for recurring subscription fees and purchase intent at a price 20% above the standard model.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.why_behaviour_changes: Smart home integration and subscription model reduce upfront cost and provide ongoing value, making the appliance attractive for occasional use.

X1.name: Smart vs Premium Subscription Test
X1.method: Online survey with two parallel arms: Arm A offers a smart, subscription-based combi-steamer at a fixed price; Arm B offers a premium, high-performance combi-steamer at a fixed price. Participants are randomly assigned to one arm. Both arms include a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question and a purchase intent question.
X1.sample: 500 adult home cooks (aged 25-55) recruited via an online panel, balanced across both arms.
X1.measure: 1) Percentage of participants who indicate they would purchase the device at the given price. 2) Average WTP (in euros) for each arm. 3) Purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A will show at least 30% purchase intent and an average WTP at least 20% of the device price, indicating demand for a subscription-based model. Arm B will show lower purchase intent and lower WTP.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B will show at least 25% purchase intent and an average WTP at least 20% of the device price, indicating demand for a premium, high-performance model. Arm A will show lower purchase intent and lower WTP.

X1.decision_rule: If Arm A’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its average WTP is at least 20% of the device price, proceed with a subscription-based home‑cook proposition. If Arm B’s purchase intent is at least 25% and its average WTP is at least 20% of the device price, proceed with a premium, high‑performance home‑cook proposition. If neither arm meets its threshold, do not expand into either segment.

revisions.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cook demand for a subscription-based combi-steamer or their willingness to pay recurring fees. It tests coordination friction, not subscription willingness to pay, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing B2B reputation and smart home integration capabilities. The test should validate willingness to pay for recurring subscription fees and purchase intent at a price 20% above the standard model.
final.target_customer: Home cooks (aged 25‑55) who value convenience, recurring value, and are open to smart home integration.
final.value_proposition: A subscription‑based combi-steamer that automates cooking, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing value, reducing upfront cost and offering recurring revenue for RATIONAL.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Smart vs Premium Subscription Test (500 participants, 6 weeks, €8,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the subscription model.
final.uncertainty: The test will determine whether home cooks are willing to pay recurring subscription fees and whether the subscription model can be scaled without cannibalizing professional sales. The source does not provide evidence of demand for a smart,
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent below 30% or average willingness to pay below 20% of the device price, the recommendation would shift to a premium, high‑performance model.
If additional evidence shows strong demand for smart home integration and recurring revenue, the recommendation would be to prioritize a subscription‑based model.
If the test confirms strong brand prestige and performance as primary drivers, the recommendation would be to emphasize premium positioning.

arguments.name: Smart vs Premium Subscription Test
arguments.method: Online survey with two parallel arms: Arm A offers a smart, subscription-based combi-steamer at a fixed price; Arm B offers a premium, high-performance combi-steamer at a fixed price. Participants are randomly assigned to one arm. Both arms include a willingness-to-pay (WTP) question and a purchase intent question.
arguments.sample: 500 adult home cooks (aged 25-55) recruited via an online panel, balanced across both arms.
arguments.measure: 1) Percentage of participants who indicate they would purchase the device at the given price. 2) Average WTP (in euros) for each arm. 3) Purchase intent on a 7-point scale (1‑2 "Very unlikely" to 7 "Very likely").

prediction_by_theory.T1: Arm A will show at least 30% purchase intent and an average WTP at least 20% of the device price, indicating demand for a subscription-based model. Arm B will show lower purchase intent and lower WTP.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Arm B will show at least 25% purchase intent and an average WTP at least 20% of the device price, indicating demand for a premium, high-performance model. Arm A will show lower purchase intent and lower WTP.

arguments.decision_rule: If Arm A’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its average WTP is at least 20% of the device price, proceed with a subscription-based home‑cook proposition. If Arm B’s purchase intent is at least 25% and its average WTP is at least 20% of the device price, proceed with a premium, high‑performance home‑cook proposition. If neither arm meets its threshold, do not expand into either segment.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated subscription-based combi-steamer proposition for home cooks, leveraging RATIONAL’s existing B2B reputation and smart home integration capabilities. The test should validate willingness to pay for recurring subscription fees and purchase intent at a price 20% above the standard model.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cook demand for a subscription-based combi-steamer or their willingness to pay recurring fees. It tests coordination friction, not subscription willingness to pay, so it does not affect T1.

The test should validate willingness to pay for recurring subscription fees and purchase intent at a price 20% above the standard model.
arguments.target_customer: Home cooks (aged 25‑55) who value convenience, recurring value, and are open to smart home integration.
arguments.value_proposition: A subscription‑based combi-steamer that automates cooking, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing value, reducing upfront cost and offering recurring revenue for RATIONAL.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Smart vs Premium Subscription Test (500 participants, 6 weeks, €8,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the subscription model.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.

alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
tool_result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 72 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 32 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cooks' willingness to pay for a smart, connected combi-steamer or their preference for convenience over traditional methods. It tests coordination friction, not consumer preferences. Therefore it does not affect T1.

would_change_if: If the test shows the premium/combi-steamer’s purchase intent and WTP exceed the smart/combi-steamer’s by at least 10 percentage points and its WTP is at least 20% above the smart’s WTP, we would shift to a premium positioning.

If a separate consumer survey revealed that home cooks prioritize durability and professional-grade performance over convenience, we would reconsider the smart positioning and explore a premium, durable model.
If the simulated test showed no meaningful difference in purchase intent or WTP between the two positions, we would recommend no expansion and maintain the current B2B focus.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).

T1.claim: Home cooks adopt combi-steamers mainly for convenience and convenience savings, not for gourmet performance, so they will pay more for a branded home unit only if it is positioned as a premium, convenience-driven product.
T1.who_benefits: Rational AG benefits by charging a premium price and selling directly to consumers through its own retail channels.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers switch from traditional cooking to combi-steamers when a single device replaces multiple appliances, saving time and effort. If they perceive a product as high-end and convenient, they are willing to pay more.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Rational AG captures value by selling premium-priced home units through its own brand, retaining margin and building consumer loyalty.
assumptions: Home cooks already own at least one traditional cooking appliance and are aware of combi-steamers.
A premium positioning can be achieved without compromising the device's performance for home use.
Consumers are willing to pay a higher price for convenience and brand reputation.
predictions: In a test offering a premium-priced home combi-steamer, purchase intent among home cooks will be higher than for a standard-combi-steamers.
Willingness to pay will be significantly higher for the premium-priced unit compared to a standard unit.
Surveyed home cooks will cite convenience and time-saving as primary purchase drivers.
T1.first_claim: Home cooks adopt combi-steamers mainly for convenience and convenience savings, not for gourmet performance, so they will pay more for a branded home unit only if it is positioned as a premium, convenience-driven product.

T2.claim: Home cooks adopt combi-steamers mainly for gourmet performance and professional-quality cooking, so they will pay more for a branded home unit only if it delivers superior cooking results compared to traditional methods.
T2.who_benefits: Rational AG benefits by positioning its home units as premium, high-performance appliances and charging a premium price for superior cooking outcomes.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: Consumers switch to combi-steamers when they perceive a device that can achieve professional-quality results, such as even cooking, precise temperature control, and reduced cooking time.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Rational AG captures value by selling premium-priced home units through its own brand, leveraging its reputation for professional-grade cooking and justifying higher margins.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to invest in a device that promises professional-quality cooking results.

Consumers are willing to pay a premium for a product that offers superior cooking outcomes.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

X1.name: Subscription vs Premium Messaging Test
X1.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a subscription-based smart combi-steamer description emphasizing automation and recurring revenue; Group B sees a premium, professional‑grade combi-steamer description emphasizing durability and performance. Both groups are shown a product description and a willingness‑to‑pay price point (proposed at €1,500). Participants indicate intent to purchase and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.
X1.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and maximum willingness‑to‑pay (in euros).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B (at least 30% intent and €1,200+ willingness to pay).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A (at least 30% intent and €1,200+ willingness to pay).

X1.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its willingness to pay is at least €1,200, proceed with the subscription‑based smart combi-steamer development. If Group B’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its willingness to pay is at least €1,200, proceed with the premium‑priced professional‑grade combi-steamer development. If neither condition is met, do not expand into either segment and maintain current B2B focus.

arguments.name: Subscription vs Premium Messaging Test
arguments.method: Online survey with randomized messaging exposure. Participants are recruited from a panel of home cooks (n=500). Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Group A sees a subscription-based smart combi-steamer description emphasizing automation and recurring revenue; Group B sees a premium, professional‑grade combi-steamer description emphasizing durability and performance. Both groups are shown a product description and a willingness‑to‑pay price point (proposed at €1,500). Participants indicate intent to purchase and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 500 home cooks recruited from an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and geographic regions.
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (binary: would purchase) and maximum willingness‑to‑pay (in euros).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Group A will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group B (at least 30% intent and €1,200+ willingness to pay).
prediction_by_theory.T2: Group B will show higher purchase intent and willingness to pay than Group A (at least 30% intent and €1,200+ willingness to pay).

arguments.decision_rule: If Group A’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its willingness to pay is at least €1,200, proceed with the subscription‑based smart combi-steamer development. If Group B’s purchase intent is at least 30% and its willingness to pay is at least €1,200, proceed with the premium‑priced professional‑grade combi-steamer development. If neither condition is met, do not expand into either segment and maintain current B2B focus.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a full-scale development yet. The evidence shows RATIONAL is a commercial kitchen leader with strong B2B performance, but it does not address home cook demand for a subscription-based combi-steamer. A small, low‑cost test (e.g., the proposed subscription vs premium messaging test) is needed to validate willingness to pay before any investment.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cook demand for a subscription-based combi-steamer. It tests coordination friction, not subscription willingness to pay. Therefore it does not affect T1.

arguments.recommendation: Do not commit to a full-scale development yet. tool_result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
tool_result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.

position.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition built on the existing combi-steamer technology, leveraging the subscription model to capture recurring revenue and convenience-driven demand.

frame.objective: Determine whether RATIONAL AG should develop a differentiated proposition for home cooks using its commercial combi-steamer technology, or remain focused on professional kitchens, based on evidence of market demand, competitive positioning, and feasibility within budget and time constraints.
constraints: Limited to public sources; no internal company data available.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must demonstrate demand, willingness to pay, or competitive advantage for either home‑cook or professional‑kitchen segments.
Any recommendation must be justified by observable data, not assumptions.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated home‑cook proposition (e.g., compact, smart, or subscription‑based combi‑steamer for residential use).
2) Stay focused on professional kitchens (no new home‑cook offering).
3) Expand into both segments (home and professional) with separate product lines or marketing.
4) No expansion (maintain current B2B focus).
5) License the combi‑steamer technology to third‑party manufacturers for residential use.

T1.who_benefits: Home cooks gain time and reduced effort; RATIONAL benefits from recurring subscription fees and higher margins.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: Smart home integration and subscription model reduce upfront cost and provide ongoing value, making the appliance attractive to tech-savvy consumers.
T1.how_value_is_captured: RATIONAL captures value through subscription revenue and premium pricing for smart features.
assumptions: Home cooks are willing to pay recurring fees for smart cooking features.
Smart home integration is accessible and affordable for residential users.
Subscription model can be scaled without significant additional capital.
predictions: In a test offering a smart, subscription-based combi-steamer, at least 30% of surveyed home cooks will sign up for the subscription within 12 weeks.
Willingness to pay for the subscription will be at least 20% of the device's price, indicating a clear paywall.

Marketing can effectively communicate the appliance's performance and durability.
Premium pricing is feasible without cannibalizing existing commercial sales.
predictions: In a test offering a premium, high-performance combi-steamer, at least 25% of surveyed home cooks will express intent to purchase at a price 20% above the standard model.
Surveyed home cooks will rank cooking performance as the top reason for purchasing, above convenience or price.

X1.name: Smart vs Premium Subscription Test
X1.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Smart Group (smart, subscription-based combi-steamer) or Premium Group (premium, high-performance combi-steamer). Both groups see the same product description and price. Smart Group also receives a recurring subscription offer with a 12-week trial. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay.
X1.sample: 500 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced across both groups (250 per group).
X1.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willingness to pay for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Smart Group will have higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a subscription than Premium Group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium Group will have higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Smart Group.

X1.decision_rule: If Smart Group purchase intent >= 30% and Premium Group purchase intent < 20%, recommend developing a differentiated home-cook proposition (T1). If Premium Group purchase intent >= 30% and Smart Group purchase intent < 20%, recommend a premium, high-performance proposition (T2). If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.

revisions.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cooks' willingness to pay for a subscription-based combi-steamer or the demand for a subscription model. It tests coordination friction, not subscription demand, so it does not affect T1.

final.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition built on the existing combi-steamer technology, leveraging a subscription model to capture recurring revenue and convenience-driven demand.
final.target_customer: Home cooks who value convenience, time-saving, and recurring revenue, particularly those who already use traditional cooking appliances.
final.value_proposition: A smart, subscription-based combi-steamer that automates cooking, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing value, offering a lower upfront cost and continuous service compared to a premium, high-performance appliance.
final.next_action: Run the proposed Smart vs Premium Subscription Test (500 home cooks, 12 weeks, €20,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the subscription-based model versus a premium, high-performance model.
final.uncertainty: The test will determine whether home cooks are willing to pay a recurring subscription fee and whether the subscription model will generate sufficient demand to justify development. The test does not address premium pricing or the size of
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the subscription-based model below 30% or willingness to pay below 20% of the device's price, the recommendation would shift to a premium, high-performance proposition (T2).

If additional evidence shows strong demand for premium features or that home cooks are unwilling to pay recurring fees, the recommendation would shift to no expansion or a different value proposition.

arguments.name: Smart vs Premium Subscription Test
arguments.method: Online survey with simulated purchase offer. Participants are randomly assigned to one of two groups: Smart Group (smart, subscription-based combi-steamer) or Premium Group (premium, high-performance combi-steamer). Both groups see the same product description and price. Smart Group also receives a recurring subscription offer with a 12-week trial. Participants indicate purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price they would pay.
arguments.sample: 500 adult home cooks recruited via an online panel, balanced across both groups (250 per group).
arguments.measure: Purchase intent (yes/no) and maximum price willingness to pay for each group.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Smart Group will have higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a subscription than Premium Group.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Premium Group will have higher purchase intent and willingness to pay a premium than Smart Group.

arguments.decision_rule: If Smart Group purchase intent >= 30% and Premium Group purchase intent < 20%, recommend developing a differentiated home-cook proposition (T1). If Premium Group purchase intent >= 30% and Smart Group purchase intent < 20%, recommend a premium, high-performance proposition (T2). If neither condition is met, recommend no expansion.

result.note: Proposed only. Nothing has been run, and its figures are analyst assumptions.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition built on the existing combi-steamer technology, leveraging the subscription model to capture recurring revenue and convenience-driven demand.

result.title: Simulated installation-coordination offer test
result.excerpt: SIMULATED RESULT, NOT REAL DATA. No study was conducted. Treat this as a what-if only. In a hypothetical randomized offer test, 800 recruited home cooks considering the same professional-derived combi-steamer were assigned equally to two offers. Both showed identical equipment, brand, cooking specifications, total installed price, warranty, available delivery dates and eventual plumbing/electrical work. One offer bundled an installation coordinator and a site-readiness checklist; the other required the purchaser to arrange the same qualified installers directly. Contact time was matched and neither offer gave a discount. All recruited homes were eligible for the stated installation work. The outcome was a paid refundable reservation remaining uncancelled after 30 days among all 400 assigned households per arm. There were 32 reservations for the coordinated-installation offer and 72 for the purchaser-arranged offer. This tests whether coordination friction changes choice in that recruited group. It does not show that the appliance fits ordinary kitchens, eliminates drain or power requirements, earns a margin, or justifies diverting resources from professional customers. It does not establish market size or a need for new RATIONAL hardware. A business recommendation can remain unchanged while belief about this narrow coordination mechanism changes.
result.access_limitation: Entirely hypothetical case-author construction; no study was conducted.

arguments.reason: The simulated installation-coordination offer test (SYN-RATIONAL-UPDATE) does not address home cooks' willingness to pay for a subscription-based combi-steamer or the demand for a subscription model. It tests coordination friction, not subscription demand, so it does not affect T1.
arguments.new_claim: Home cooks will adopt a differentiated combi-steamer if it is marketed as a smart, subscription-based device that automates cooking and delivers recipes, because they value convenience and recurring revenue.

arguments.recommendation: Develop a differentiated home-cook proposition built on the existing combi-steamer technology, leveraging a subscription model to capture recurring revenue and convenience-driven demand.
arguments.target_customer: Home cooks who value convenience, time-saving, and recurring revenue, particularly those who already use traditional cooking appliances.
arguments.value_proposition: A smart, subscription-based combi-steamer that automates cooking, delivers recipes, and provides ongoing value, offering a lower upfront cost and continuous service compared to a premium, high-performance appliance.
arguments.next_action: Run the proposed Smart vs Premium Subscription Test (500 home cooks, 12 weeks, €20,000) to measure purchase intent and willingness to pay for the subscription-based model versus a premium, high-performance model.
arguments.uncertainty: The test will determine whether home cooks are willing to pay a recurring subscription fee and whether the subscription model will generate sufficient demand to justify development. The test does not address premium pricing or the size of
would_change_if: If the test shows purchase intent for the subscription-based model below 30% or willingness to pay below 20% of the device's price, the recommendation would shift to a premium, high-performance proposition (T2).

If additional evidence shows strong demand for premium features or that home cooks are unwilling to pay recurring fees, the recommendation would shift to no expansion or a different value proposition.
